blocks.prompt: The Hunter That Waits
blocks.text: A praying mantis is a hunter that waits. It does not chase. It stands on a stem, green as the leaves around it, and holds its front legs up in a fold. Those legs are not folded for praying. They are folded for grabbing. Each one has a row of tiny spines along the inside. When a fly lands nearby, the mantis snaps its legs out and pulls the fly in. The whole grab takes less time than a blink. A mantis can also turn its head around to look behind itself. No other insect can do that.

blocks.prompt: The Hunter That Never Chases
blocks.text: Most hunters run. A praying mantis does the opposite. It picks a stem or a leaf, matches the green or brown around it, and then it stops moving. It can hold that pose for an hour. Its front legs are folded in front of its face, which is how it got its name. Those legs are the trap. The inside edge of each one carries a row of sharp spines. When an insect wanders close enough, the mantis throws both legs forward and pulls the insect back onto the spines. The strike takes about fifty thousandths of a second. If you blink, you miss it. The mantis can also do something no other insect can do. It can swivel its head and look over its own shoulder. Most insects have a stiff neck and have to turn their whole body to see behind them. A mantis just turns its triangle of a head, keeps the rest of itself perfectly still, and watches you watching it.

notes: The black dot in each eye is a pseudopupil, not a pupil
The only insect known to see in 3D

blocks.prompt: Ambush, Disguise, and a Dot That Follows You
blocks.text: A praying mantis hunts with its eyes, and its eyes are strange even by insect standards. Look at one closely and you will see a small black dot in each big eye, and the dot seems to follow you around the room. That dot is not a pupil. It is called a pseudopupil, and it is simply the tunnel of eye tubes pointing straight back at you, swallowing the light instead of reflecting it. Wherever you stand, the tubes aimed at you look dark. Behind those eyes is something rarer. The mantis is the only insect known to see in true three dimensions. It compares the slightly different view from each eye and works out exactly how far away its target is, the same way you do. Scientists at a lab in England tested this by fitting mantises with tiny colored glasses and showing them 3D movies of bugs. The mantises struck at empty air where the fake bug appeared to be. That is proof the depth was in their heads, not in the room. Distance matters because a mantis only gets one try. It does not chase. It waits, disguised. Some species look like green leaves, some like dead brown leaves, some like sticks. The orchid mantis of Southeast Asia looks like a pink flower, and it works so well that insects fly to it instead of to real flowers. The disguise is not for hiding. It is bait.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: One ear, on the belly, between the hind legs
Tuned to ultrasound, the range bats shout in

blocks.prompt: One Ear, Aimed at the Dark
blocks.text: Nearly every animal you can name keeps its ears on its head, and keeps two of them, because two is how you tell which direction a sound came from. The praying mantis broke both rules. It has exactly one ear, and the ear is not on its head. It sits in a groove on the underside of the body, between the back legs, a slot deep enough to hide a pin. One ear cannot locate anything. It cannot tell left from right, or in front from behind. For most purposes that would make it useless. But this ear was not built for most purposes. It is tuned almost entirely to ultrasound, to frequencies far above anything you can hear, and in the night sky there is really only one thing making that sound: a hunting bat. A bat finds its food by shouting and listening for the echo. A flying mantis hears the shout coming. It does not need to know where the bat is. It only needs to know that a bat is somewhere, and that it has very little time to stop being where it is. So the mantis folds up its legs, tips its head, and drops. Sometimes it spirals. Sometimes it dives straight into the grass. Scientists have watched this in the dark with high-speed cameras, and mantises that dive survive bat attacks far more often than mantises that fly on. Here is the part that makes the ear a puzzle worth thinking about. The ear is useless to the females of many species, because those females are too heavy to fly at all. They still have it. And the ear appears in mantis history roughly when bats do, tens of millions of years after mantises themselves. The mantis did not grow an ear to hear the world. It grew an ear to hear one enemy.

meta.templateLabel: The Bug That Can Look Over Its Shoulder

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Mantodea, roughly 2,400 species
Greek mantis means prophet or seer
Raptorial front legs, hinged and spined
Strike lands in about fifty milliseconds
Closest living relatives: cockroaches and termites
Sexual cannibalism happens in a minority of matings

blocks.prompt: The Patience Machine
blocks.text: Every animal that hunts has to solve the same problem: how do you get close to something that does not want you close? Wolves solve it by running. Spiders solve it by building. The praying mantis solves it by disappearing while standing in plain sight, and then by being faster, for one twentieth of a second, than anything nearby can react to. Start with the name, because the name is a mistake. Early European naturalists watched the insect hold its folded front legs up beneath its face and decided it was at prayer. The Greek word mantis means prophet or seer, and for centuries people believed a mantis could point a lost child home. What the insect is actually doing is loading a weapon. Each front leg is a raptorial leg, hinged like a pocket knife, with two rows of hooked spines that close against each other. Held up under the head, the legs are not resting. They are cocked. The strike takes somewhere near fifty milliseconds, faster than your eye can follow and faster than a fly can launch. The mantis does not simply snap shut, either. High-speed film shows it adjusting its reach mid strike, correcting for the fly's own movement in the fraction of a moment while the legs are still traveling. This is why the eyes matter so much. A mantis judges distance in true three dimensions, comparing the view from each eye, and it is the only insect ever shown to do so. When researchers fitted mantises with tiny colored 3D glasses and played them movies, the insects struck at empty air. The rest of the animal is built around the waiting rather than the strike. Its shape is a lie: green leaf, dead leaf, twig, lichen, bark, and in the case of the orchid mantis of Southeast Asia, a pink and white flower so convincing that pollinators fly to it in preference to actual blossoms. The disguise is not defensive. It is a lure. The head swivels almost halfway around on a flexible neck, so the body never has to move and give the game away. And underneath, between the hind legs, sits a single ear tuned to the ultrasonic shouts of hunting bats, the one thing a patient insect cannot out-wait. Folklore has never quite forgiven the mantis. It is widely believed that the female always eats the male, and that killing a mantis is against the law. Neither is true. Field studies find cannibalism in a minority of matings, and it is more common in laboratory tanks where the female is hungry and the male cannot leave. The mantis has never been protected by law in the United States, despite how often people repeat that it is. What is true is stranger than the stories. The mantis is not a close cousin of the grasshopper. Its nearest living relatives are cockroaches and termites. Somewhere back in that shared family tree, a roach-like ancestor stopped scavenging, raised its front legs, learned to hold still, and became the most patient predator in the garden.
